burden_of_proof: The burden of proof rests on the party proposing a departure from the Masoretic pointing, as the Masoretic tradition is a highly conservative, meticulously transmitted ancient reading tradition.
required_support: Grammatical and morphological validity of the proposed vocalization within Biblical Hebrew
Coherence with the immediate literary and syntactic context
Evidence from ancient versions (e.g., Septuagint, Peshitta, Vulgate, Targumim) reflecting the alternate vocalization
Manuscript evidence (e.g., Dead Sea Scrolls) demonstrating variant orthography or spacing
ketiv_qere_rule: The Ketiv represents the older transmitted consonantal text, while the Qere represents the official oral reading tradition of the Masoretes. Neither is automatically binding over the other; the Ketiv is often prioritized for reconstructing the oldest written text, whereas the Qere may preserve legitimate ancient corrections, morphological standardizations, or euphemisms. Both must be weighed contextually.
ancient_witness_rule: Ancient translations and variant manuscripts can provide evidence of alternate vocalizations or differing pre-Masoretic consonantal base texts (Vorlagen). Their testimony is admissible and valuable but must be critically evaluated against the specific translation techniques, theological tendencies, and historical provenances of each witness.
historical_findings: Biblical Hebrew was initially recorded as a purely consonantal text without written vowels.
Vowel letters (matres lectionis) were slowly incorporated over time to assist reading.
The Masoretic vowel points (niqqud) and cantillation marks (te'amim) were created and standardized centuries later (circa 600-1000 CE) to preserve the oral tradition.
Ancient Greek and Aramaic translations frequently attest to reading traditions that vocalized the consonants differently than the later Masoretic text.
theological_assumptions: The assertion that the Masoretic vowel points are co-eval with the consonants and equally inspired is a historically recent theological assumption (e.g., 17th-century Protestant scholasticism) rather than a manuscript-based fact.
The doctrine of perfect textual preservation without scribal variations is a theological premise distinct from the historical reality of textual transmission.
rationale: Because the Masoretic vowel points and cantillation marks were introduced centuries after the original composition of the biblical texts, they constitute an ancient, reliable, but inherently interpretive overlay upon the original consonantal text. Consequently, they establish a strong presumption of the correct reading, but they are not an absolute veto against grammatically valid alternate vocalizations that possess compelling contextual and historical support.
